Prologue.

It is a well-known thing that the astrologers called Genethliaci are diligent in knowing the hour and exact moment of each person's birth: with this knowledge they divine and predict the natural inclinations of men, by consideration of the sign under which they are born, and of the state and aspect that the planets then had among themselves and in relation to the sign. These astrologers, or diviners, base their divination on the influence of the constellations and planets; and for this reason their divination is tolerated, and permitted in the almanacs that common people use, on the condition that no one should think that the influence of the constellation does anything more than incline one toward sensuality, and that it has no power whatsoever over free will.

The natives of all New Spain had, and still have, great diligence in knowing the day and hour of each person's birth, in order to divine the character, life, and death of those who were born. Those who held this office were called tonalpouhque, and to them people turned as if to prophets, whenever a son or daughter was born, to be informed about their character, life, and death. These diviners were not guided by the signs or planets of the sky, but by a set of instructions which, according to them, was left by Quetzalcoatl, which contains twenty characters multiplied thirteen times, in the manner set forth in the present book. This kind of divination cannot in any way be licit, because it is not based on the influence of the stars, nor on anything natural, nor does its cycle conform to the cycle of the year, since it contains no more than two hundred and sixty days, after which it begins again from the start. This device is either a continuous artifice, or an art of necromancy, or a pact and fabrication of the devil, which must be rooted out with all diligence.

To the sincere reader.

In the present volume, friend reader, you have all the movable feasts of the year in their order, and the ceremonies, sacrifices, rejoicings, and superstitions that were practiced on them; from which one may take indication and warning in order to know whether these are now observed wholly or in part — although, since the time at which they occur is not known, being movable feasts, it will be difficult to fall upon them exactly. You also have here a great deal of vocabulary pertaining to this subject, matter well worn among them but quite hidden from us. There is occasion in this subject matter to judge the ability of these people; it contains, though briefly, some rather delicate things, as can be seen in the table found at the end of the book.

Book Four

Book Four, of judicial astrology, or the art of divination, which these Mexicans used in order to know which days were well-fortuned and which were ill-fortuned, and what conditions those born on the days attributed to the characters or signs set forth here would have; and it seems to be a matter of necromancy rather than of astrology.

Chapter One, of the first sign, called Ce Cipactli, and of the good fortune that those born under it had — both men and women — unless they lost it through their own negligence or laxity.

Here begin the characters of each day, which were reckoned in periods of thirteen (trecenas): there were thirteen days in each "week," and they formed a circle of two hundred [and sixty days]...

[Parallel Nahuatl text:]

This is the fourth book: it speaks of the book of days (the tonalamatl), which the Mexica consulted for guidance; and thus said the day-counters — whether a day was good or not good — by it the fate of the day was signified, here it is called [as follows]: and what would befall the one who was born under it. And this book of days is, in truth, more properly called the tonalpohualli (count of days), by which especially they reckoned.

Chapter One: it speaks concerning the first sign, called Ce Cipactli, and of the good fortune merited by those born under it, men and women — unless they themselves lost it, bringing it upon themselves through their own laziness.

Here begins the count of days: just as a single week was counted, so thirteen days were made into one such period.

[Nahuatl text — continuation of the day-count calendar system, describing how the trecena (thirteen-day period) proceeds through the year, beginning with the sign Ce Cipactli (One Crocodile), and listing the sequence of day-signs: Ome Acatl (Two Reed), Ei Calli (Three House), Nahui Cuetzpalin (Four Lizard), Macuilli Coatl (Five Serpent), Chicuace Miquiztli (Six Death), Chicome Mazatl (Seven Deer), Chicuei Tochtli (Eight Rabbit), Chiconahui Atl (Nine Water), Matlactli Itzcuintli (Ten Dog), Matlactli once Ozomatli (Eleven Monkey), Matlactli omome Malinalli (Twelve Grass), Matlactli omei Acatl (Thirteen Reed). It explains that whoever is born under certain of these signs — such as the nobleman born under favorable signs — will become a ruler, will be obeyed, will prosper and be given things; while one born under an unfavorable sign will become a brave warrior, feared, who will rise up and achieve renown through valor, yet one born under other such signs will not be obeyed.]

Of the art of divination. Folio 2.

...which means "rabbit." The ninth day is of another character, called atl, which means "water." The tenth day is of another character, called ocomatli, which means "monkey." The eleventh day is of another character, called itzcuintli, which means "dog." The twelfth day is of another character, called malinalli, which means "grass/hay." The thirteenth day is of another character, called acatl, which means "cane."

These thirteen days, they said, were very fortunate, so that whoever was born on any of these thirteen days—if he were the son of a nobleman—would be a lord or a senator, and rich. And if he were the son of humble fortune and poor parents, he would be brave, honored, and respected by all, and would have enough to eat. And if a girl were born on any of these thirteen days, she would be rich and would have everything necessary for her household: for spending on food and drink, for giving feasts, for dancing, and for holding gatherings in her house; and she would give food and drink to the poor, the elderly, and orphans who have nothing to eat or drink, and she would be prosperous...

[The accompanying Nahuatl text, corresponding to this Spanish passage, describes the same ideas in the original language: it speaks of becoming wealthy, being honored and served, having food and drink provided, being comforted in old age, and the good fortune — or in other cases, misfortune and suffering, including hardship, poverty, illness, and need — that could come to those born under these day-signs, according to Aztec belief in fate tied to the calendar.]

Book 4.

...what he did, by his work, in order to earn his living: and nothing of his labor will be lost to him: and he will be skillful at selling all kinds of merchandise, and at earning as much as he can. And moreover they said: that even though, at the moment of a child's birth, it had a very fortunate character, if it did not do penance, and if it was not corrected, and if it did not endure the punishments that are given to it, and the jealous and harsh words that are spoken to it—and if it is poorly raised and does not walk the straight path—it loses everything that it had deserved through the good sign under which it was born. Such a person despises himself and blinds himself, even if he takes up with a concubine. He loses the good fortune he had, and so he becomes poor, and has nothing to eat or drink, and will suffer great hardship all his life; because he himself brought misfortune upon himself through his own wickedness, being disobedient, arrogant, and careless. He will find contentment nowhere, and will always live in poverty and misfortune. Everyone will despise him, everyone will hold him as worthless, no one will take him as a friend, he will wander alone, no one will love him, and everywhere people will wish him ill and speak evil of him. He is hateful to everyone, and...

[The parallel Nahuatl text continues the same account in the Nahuatl language, describing how such a person is scorned and reviled, how he brings shame and disgrace upon himself through his own vice and wickedness, how no one shows him friendship, how he is spoken of with contempt everywhere, how he becomes the object of gossip and slander, and how he ends up abandoned, despised, and sunk in affliction and suffering — the counterpart in Nahuatl of the preceding Spanish passage.]

del[la] arte                          divinatoria.                    folio 3.

...they looked upon him with bad eyes, for being a notorious sinner, and everyone cursed him, for being proud and a vagabond, and for going about lost and disobedient to what he was commanded and counseled, and because he did not care for proper upbringing. And when a child was born under a good sign, the fathers and mothers would say: "Our child is fortunate, and has a good sign," which is called Cipactli.
Then they would baptize him, and give him the name of the sign: they would call him Cipac, or they would give him another name from among the grandparents, etc.
And if it seemed good to them, they would postpone the baptism to another day, so that it might fall under a better fortune, within the same sign. And if the child born was a boy: when they baptized him, they made him a small shield, with four little arrows, and they tied the umbilical cord to them, and gave it all together to men who were soldiers, so that they might carry it to the place of battle, and there they buried it. And if the child born was a girl: when they baptized her, they placed in a washbasin all the implements of a woman — those with which women spin and weave — because the life of a woman is to be raised at home, and to remain and live within it: her umbilical cord they buried near the hearth.

[Parallel Nahuatl text, describing the same matters concerning the day-sign Cipactli — the manner in which one born under it might become shameless, quick-tempered, a drunkard, or hardened in wrongdoing, unable to be corrected or counseled; and how, if someone born under a fortunate day within the sign of One Crocodile (Ce Cipactli) was bathed and given his fate, the rites of washing and naming were performed accordingly, whether a new house was to be dedicated or the child was to be bathed; and if a male child was born, at the time of his bathing a small shield was made for him, and four little darts, and these were bound to his umbilical cord and hung upon him, together with other things pertaining to his future estate...]

Book 4.

And this astrology, or necromancy, was taken and had its origin from a woman called Oxomoco, and from a man called Cipactonal. And the masters of this astrology, or necromancy, who kept count of these signs, who were called tonalpouhque [day-counters]: they painted this woman Oxomoco, and this man Cipactonal, and placed them in the middle of the books, where all the characters of each day were written; for they said that these two were the lords of this astrology, or necromancy, as the principal astrologers, because they had invented and made this count of all the characters.

[Image: two seated figures on a woven mat, a man and a woman, with small objects laid out between them, apparently performing a divination]

Chapter two, of the second sign, called ce...

[Nahuatl text, parallel to the Spanish, describing the ritual practices associated with the calendar: the laying out of offerings, the spinning and weaving implements (spindle, cotton, weaving materials) placed before the deity, the washing basins and vessels set out, and the account of how the day-count (tonalpoalli) came to be. It is said that the elders declared that it was those two, named Oxomoco and Cipactonal, who gave light and knowledge to the people, the two revered ones. Oxomoco the woman made the paintings and the count, and Cipactonal the man was likewise a day-counter; together their erudition established and ordered the sacred count, setting the images in their proper arrangement, and from them the rulers and all things pertaining to the day-count were derived.]

Chapter two: concerning what pertains to this, the second thing that is told...

Of the divinatory art.

...ocelotl, and of the bad fortune that those born under it had, both men and women: if with their diligence they did not remedy it, those born under this sign were for the most part slaves.

The second character is called ocelotl, which means "tiger" [jaguar]: this one reigned for another thirteen days. They said it was an unfortunate sign during all the thirteen days it governed. This ocelotl held the first house, or day. The second held quauhtli, which means "eagle." The third held cozcaquauh, which means another large bird so called. The fourth held olin, which means "movement." The fifth held tecpatl, which means "flint." The sixth held quiauitl, which means "rain." The seventh held xochitl, which means "flower." The eighth held cipactli, which...

...[the Nahuatl text continues, describing] belongs to one ocelotl: and [it was said] it was not a good day-sign; one who was born in it, a woman, [would suffer] trouble; and by it the destiny was shown, one could not easily be cured of it. And whoever was born in it, nearly everyone, would turn out poorly.

Thus the thirteen-day period begins, named One Ocelotl. When it began, it was said it was not a good day sign, a sign of ferocity, a sign of seizing and taking captives, and there spread out the thirteen [day-signs] belonging to it: namely, two Eagle, three Vulture, four Movement, five Flint, six Rain, seven Flower, eight Crocodile (Cipactli), nine Wind, ten House, eleven Lizard, twelve Serpent, thirteen Death: and whoever was born under it, [it was said], a noble, or a commoner — it was said, [that it meant] death in war, destruction, captivity, imprisonment...

[It] means swordfish. The ninth sign had Ehecatl, which means wind. The tenth had Calli, which means house. The eleventh had Cuetzpalin, which means lizard. The twelfth had Coatl, which means serpent. The thirteenth had Miquiztli, which means death.

Whoever was born—whether noble or commoner—under any of these houses (signs), it was said that he would have to be a captive in war, and in all his affairs he would be unfortunate and vicious, and very given to women; and even if he became a brave man, in the end he would sell himself into slavery. And this he did because he was born under such a sign. But they also said that even though he was born under such an unlucky sign, he could remedy this through the skill and diligence he showed: by not sleeping much, doing penance, fasting, and piercing himself to draw blood from his body, and sweeping the house where he was raised,

[The Nahuatl text on the right column parallels and elaborates upon the same subject matter as the Spanish text—describing the fates, customs, and penitential practices associated with those born under these day-signs, including references to captivity, sacrifice, labor, abstinence, and ritual duties performed to counteract ill fortune.]

Soothsaying. Folio 5.

[The following Nahuatl text parallels the Spanish account, describing how the diviners watched over and sought out a person's fate and destiny according to this day-sign: whether he would wake well or ill, what sickness might befall him, how he would provide for his children, whether misfortune, poverty, or shame would follow him, and whether he would live virtuously or fall into wrongdoing. It likewise tells how, if a noblewoman was born under this sign, it was said she would become an adulteress and would be put to death by stoning between two stones, and that she would live in poverty, suffering, and disgrace all her days.]

Book 4.

honored this sign, which
is called Xochitl: and they made for it a

also the women who were embroiderers
honored this sign, and fasted:
eighty, or forty,
or twenty days before, so that they would
arrive at the feast on this sign Xochitl: for
the reason that they asked it to give them,
and favor them in their labors
of fine embroidery: and to the women,

[The Nahuatl text parallels the Spanish, describing the day sign and its associated beliefs: that it governed one's fate upon this earth, determining whether a person would be fortunate or unfortunate, brave or cowardly, destined for captivity or war. It speaks of the sign Nahui Ollin (Four Movement), which was greatly venerated by Motecuhzoma; when this sign arose, incense was burned and offerings made before the image of the sun called Cuecaltonameyotl. At midday captives were sacrificed. It states that whoever was born under this sign had no fixed destiny — he might become a warrior or go off to war. They said that thus the sun was sustained, and so all people performed penance at that time: one day of bloodletting was observed by everyone, without exception, whether man, woman, or child; they pierced their ears and offered their blood, as was customary.]

Of the art
of weaving well and working well: and they placed lights and incense, and killed quail before the statue. And, the fast having passed, all bathed themselves in order to celebrate the feast of the said sign Seven Flower (Chicome Xochitl), and they said that this sign was also an unlucky one: that any woman weaver who broke the fast would become, and deserved to become, a public woman. And they said further that weaver-women were nearly all of bad conduct in their bodies, by reason of what happened, at the origin of weaving, with the goddess Xochiquetzal, who deceived them. And this goddess also gave them incurable scabs and pox, and other contagious diseases; and she who did penance, as she was obliged to, deserved to be a woman of good fame and honor, and would be well married.

And they said further that whoever was born under the said sign Flower (Xochitl) would be skillful in all the mechanical arts, if diligent and well brought up; and if not well brought up and understanding, neither would such a one deserve good fortune, but rather misfortunes and dishonors. The ninth house...

[The Nahuatl text, running parallel, describes the raising up of the sun; it states that concerning Seven Flower it was said both good and bad things: that it was good because in one place they honored and trusted it, where the scribes/painters made the offerings and image and gave gifts to it; also the women who did needlework and embroidery first fasted for four days, or eight days, or twenty days, asking thereby that they might become something, be prudent, be skilled, be good at crafts and skilled in making things — all in relation to the arts of painting and needlework; and all bathed and washed their heads when the feast of Seven Flower arrived there; but it was also said that it was bad, because when someone skilled in crafts committed a fault or did improper things it was said that there they merited mockery and the name of licentious; so that it was said they would live dissolutely, live vainly, and be called very dissolute and vain-living, and that craftsmen, it is said, feared her, the one who was their deity, named Xochiquetzal, and who gave gifts...]

unfortunate: because his life would be like
the wind, that carries away with it
everything it can: he wishes to be

On the Art [of soothsaying]                          [On] soothsaying.    fol. 7.

...he lived in idleness, he wandered about aimlessly, he squandered himself, he hid himself in the forest, even though he was a brave warrior: he remained poor, nothing came to him, nowhere was he to be found; it is said: nowhere could his arrow be found, nowhere his shield, nowhere could he seek his livelihood: and although it seemed he supported himself, and although it seemed he prospered, he was never content; he was just like the wind, like water that flows away, taking nothing with it, holding onto nothing, so that in vain was spent all his courage.

Here the third chapter tells of this: here is depicted the third sign, named ce mázatl (One Deer): and of the good fortune which men and women born in that time deserved and were granted; but if it was not fulfilled in them, then through their own idleness they would lose it.

Here begins the third part of the sign: this is ce mázatl, again...
